meta.titre: Magnetism: magnetic materials, testing and magnetisation
meta.sous_theme: Magnets, domains and soft and hard materials

sections.contenu_markdown: At a scrapyard in Douala, a large electromagnet lifts old iron from a heap and drops it when the current is switched off, while copper and aluminium stay behind. A fridge door stays shut because of a magnetic strip, and a loudspeaker has a strong permanent magnet. At the GCE you are asked which materials are magnetic, how to test for a magnet, how to make and destroy a magnet, and why soft iron is used in some devices and steel in others.

items: A magnet has two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract.
Metals such as iron, steel, copper and aluminium look similar but have different properties.
A freely suspended magnet comes to rest pointing roughly north-south.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Magnetic materials.** The magnetic materials are iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Copper, aluminium, brass, wood, glass and plastic are non-magnetic. A magnet attracts magnetic materials, but it does not attract non-magnetic ones.

**Law of magnetic poles and the test for a magnet.** Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. An unmagnetised piece of iron is also attracted by either pole of a magnet, so attraction alone does not prove that a bar is a magnet. **Repulsion is the only sure test**, because only another magnet can repel a pole.

**Domain theory.** A magnetic material contains many tiny magnets called domains. In an unmagnetised bar they point in all directions and cancel. In a magnet, most domains are lined up in the same direction. If a magnet is cut in two, each piece is a complete magnet with its own N and S poles.

**Making a magnet.** (1) Stroke a steel bar many times in one direction with one pole of a magnet, lifting the magnet well above the bar on each return. (2) Place the bar inside a solenoid and send a direct current through it for a short time (the electrical method is the quickest and strongest).

**Destroying a magnet (demagnetising).** (1) Hammer it. (2) Heat it until it is red hot. (3) Place it in a solenoid carrying alternating current and slowly pull it out while the current is on. In each case the domains are jumbled again.

**Soft and hard magnetic materials.** Soft iron is easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise: it makes temporary magnets. Steel is hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism: it makes permanent magnets.

variantes.nom: Soft iron or steel: which for what?
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to choose a material for an electrical device or a magnet.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use **soft iron** where the magnetism must be switched on and off: the cores of electromagnets, relays, electric bells and transformers. Use **steel** where the magnetism must last: compass needles, permanent magnets, loudspeaker magnets and the strips on fridge doors.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron or steel object.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A magnet near a piece of iron turns it into a magnet while it is near. The end of the iron nearer to the magnet gets the pole **opposite** to the nearer pole of the magnet, so the two attract. Soft iron loses its induced magnetism when the magnet is taken away, while steel keeps part of it.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how to keep magnets strong.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Bar magnets are stored in pairs with unlike poles side by side, with soft iron *keepers* across the ends. The keepers and the opposite poles form closed loops that keep the domains lined up. Magnets lose strength if they are dropped, hammered, heated or stored badly.

sections.enonce_markdown: You are given three bars, P, Q and R, which look the same. Bar P is a magnet with a marked N end. The N end of P repels one end of Q and attracts the other end of Q. Both ends of R are attracted by both ends of P, and R repels nothing. What can you say about Q and R? How would you tell if R is made of iron or of copper?

etapes.justification: Repulsion happens only between like poles of two magnets.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The N end of P repels one end of Q, so Q has a N pole at that end. The other end attracts, so it is a S pole. **Q is a magnet.**

etapes.justification: Attraction occurs between a magnet and an unmagnetised magnetic material, so it does not prove R is a magnet.
etapes.resultat_markdown: R is attracted at both ends and never repelled. **R is magnetic material that is not a magnet** (for example unmagnetised iron or steel).

etapes.justification: Copper is not magnetic and would not be attracted by either end of P.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Since R is attracted by P, **R is not copper**; it is iron, steel, nickel or cobalt.

etapes.action: Choose one more test to separate iron from steel.
etapes.justification: Soft iron loses its magnetism quickly, while steel keeps it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Stroke R with a magnet and test it with a compass. If it keeps its magnetism, it is steel; if it loses it quickly, it is soft iron.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Q is a magnet (repulsion proves it), R is an unmagnetised magnetic material, and R cannot be copper. A magnetisation test then separates soft iron from steel.

items.erreur_markdown: "The bar is attracted to a magnet, so it must be a magnet."
items.pourquoi_faux: Unmagnetised iron and steel are also attracted. Attraction occurs between unlike poles and between a magnet and any magnetic material.
items.correction_markdown: Only repulsion shows that the bar is a magnet.

items.erreur_markdown: "If I cut a magnet in half, I get one north piece and one south piece."
items.pourquoi_faux: Each piece contains many aligned domains, so each piece has both a N and S pole.
items.correction_markdown: Cutting a magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S poles.

items.erreur_markdown: "Steel is used for the core of an electromagnet because it keeps its magnetism."
items.pourquoi_faux: The core must lose its magnetism when the current is switched off. Steel would stay magnetised.
items.correction_markdown: Use soft iron for electromagnet cores and steel for permanent magnets.

items.erreur_markdown: "A magnet attracts all metals, such as copper and aluminium."
items.pourquoi_faux: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Copper and aluminium are not attracted.
items.correction_markdown: Say that a magnet attracts only magnetic materials.

items.erreur_markdown: "Heating a magnet makes it stronger because the domains move faster."
items.pourquoi_faux: Heating jumbles the domains and the magnet loses its strength.
items.correction_markdown: Heating (and hammering) are ways of demagnetising a magnet.

items.enonce_markdown: From this list, name the materials that a magnet attracts: steel, copper, nickel, plastic, cobalt, aluminium, iron, brass.
items.solution_markdown: A magnet attracts **steel, nickel, cobalt and iron**. It does not attract copper, plastic, aluminium or brass.

items.enonce_markdown: A bar of soft iron and a bar of steel of the same size are placed in turn inside a solenoid carrying a direct current. The current is switched off and both bars are brought near some iron pins. (a) State what is observed with each bar. (b) Explain the difference in terms of domains. (c) Which material would you choose for the core of an electric bell, and which for a compass needle?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The steel bar **picks up pins** because it stays magnetised; the soft iron bar **drops them** (or holds almost none).

(b) In both bars the current lines up the domains. In soft iron the domains return to random directions as soon as the current stops; in steel they stay lined up.

(c) Electric bell core: **soft iron**, because it must stop being magnetic when the current is cut. Compass needle: **steel**, because it must stay magnetised.

items.enonce_markdown: The north-seeking end of a compass needle is repelled by end A of a bar M and attracted by end B. Another bar K attracts the compass needle at both of its ends, but never repels it. (a) Identify the poles of M. (b) Decide which bar is surely a magnet and explain why the other is not proved to be one. (c) What happens when M is cut into two pieces? (d) State two ways of destroying the magnetism of M.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A N pole repels the north-seeking end of the needle, so **A is a N pole and B is a S pole**.

(b) **M is a magnet**, because it repels. K only attracts, which can also happen with unmagnetised iron or steel, so K is **not proved** to be a magnet.

(c) Each piece is a complete magnet with its own N and S poles.

(d) **Hammering** the bar, **heating** it until it is red hot, or placing it in a solenoid carrying alternating current and slowly withdrawing it.

items_markdown: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; copper, aluminium, wood and plastic are not.
Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet; attraction also occurs with unmagnetised iron or steel.
A magnet is made of aligned domains; cutting a magnet gives two complete magnets, each with N and S poles.
Make magnets by stroking in one direction or with direct current in a solenoid; destroy them by hammering, heating or alternating current.
Soft iron is used for temporary magnets and electromagnet cores; steel is used for permanent magnets and compass needles.
